features.description: The preceding context concerns Britain, the island: hit refers to it. Swilce ... ēac, also. Berende on, rich in / productive of; węcga is genitive plural “of metals,” and ōrum dative plural “veins/ores” after on. The following genitives name the metals. Āres is Cook’s source spelling for copper here, beside the earlier selected ǣr.

features.description: Gesihð is feminine accusative singular, sight/gaze; ūre agrees with it. Feorr, far off. Ūpāhōfon, we lifted up, first plural preterite of ūpāhebban. The complete phrase describes looking up and seeing at a distance.

features.description: In Farne, on Farne island, with ðǣm īglande as dative apposition. Gode ðone lēofan fæder means the father dear to God: the adjective’s complement is dative. Æðelwald is in apposition to the accusative fæder. Of + dative means out of/from; dīegelnessum is the source plural for retreat/seclusion. Ūtgangende is the printed participle, coming out; Cook notes that a present participle is used for a Latin past participle here, so “having come out” is also possible.

features.description: The ðæt clause gives his purpose. Wolde with the infinitives scēawian and gesēon is read here “that he might watch and see” or “in order to watch and see”; do not make private desire the only force. Hwæt ūs gelumpe is a dependent question, what might happen to us. Gelumpe is third singular preterite subjunctive, and ūs is dative.

features.description: For-ðon is the shorter source spelling of the causal conjunction. Gehīerde, heard, is a prefixed past form. Gebrec is the accusative noise/crash; ðǣra storma is genitive plural of storms, and ðæs weallendes sǣs genitive singular of the surging sea. Weallendes is an adjectival participle, surging/boiling. Ðǣra preserves the source genitive-plural spelling.

features.description: The temporal clause contains both scēawode and geseah. With geseah, understand the earlier ūs as the people seen: he saw us to be situated in distress and despair. features.description: The temporal clause has the two completed actions: we came up onto land and carried our ship up from the waves. Lande is the locally supplied dative of land; ȳðum is dative plural waves after fram. Ābǣron is first plural preterite of prefixed carry. Ūre scip is the accusative object, not a new subject.

features.description: Sōna, immediately; ęft, again; hwearf, returned. Se-ðe is the exact relative complex referring to masculine storm. For ūrum intingan, for our sake; intingan is dative singular. features.description: Ealne ðone dæg is accusative duration, all that day. Strang, strong, agrees with storm. The first ðætte introduces the result: people could clearly understand. features.description: Tō bēnum, at/in response to the prayers, uses dative plural. Ðæs Godes weres means of the man of God; weres is genitive singular, with Godes depending on it. For intingan ūre hǣle means for the sake of our rescue: hǣle is genitive singular; exact ūre is supplied in this possessive expression. Heofonlice means from heaven; forgiefen means given/granted here, expressly not forgiven. The final passive refers to the brief period of calm.
